stories.headline: India’s largest earthquake-isolated hospital block coming up at LD Hospital
stories.title: India’s largest earthquake-isolated hospital block coming up at LD Hospital
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 24: This building is designed to move with the earthquakes. In one of India's most earthquake-vulnerable regions, Kashmir, a major engineering initiative is shaping country's largest purpose-designed hospital structure. The six-storey structure at Lal Ded Hospital Srinagar incorporates advanced seismic base-isolation technology, and is nearing completion soon. The World Bank funded extension block at the premier maternity hospital has been conceived around earthquake-isolation technology from its design stage. Most such structures have the system introduced as a subsequent structural retrofit. The building incorporates 43 friction pendulum isolators. These are designed to reduce the transfer of seismic forces from the ground to the structure during an earthquake. The LD Hospital project is the largest among three such base-isolation projects in India. The project is among the India’s significant applications of the technology in hospital infrastructure. This project is being executed under the Jhelum and Tawi Flood Recovery Project (JTFRP). Medical Superintendent Lal Ded Hospital, Dr Muzaffar Jan said the project is an engineering marvel, not just for J&K, but for the entire country. The base-isolation system is the key and differentiating feature of the building's structural design. In conventional construction the foundation is rigidly connected to the superstructure. In base isolation system, specially engineered bearings allow controlled movement between the building and the ground during seismic activity. The friction pendulum system uses sliding bearings with curved surfaces to help dissipate earthquake energy. It also limits the forces transmitted to the structure. The 43 isolators are intended to provide an additional layer of protection to a critical healthcare facility. Dr Jan said the building can bear a quake upto the intensity of 8 Richter scale. The design and engineering components have undergone technical vetting by premier institutions. This project demonstrates a significant application of advanced seismic engineering in public healthcare infrastructure. The MS, Dr Jan, said the original allotted cost of Rs 118.22 crore has been revised to Rs 127.75 crore now. The G+5 structure with an attic has a total built-up area of 11,640 square metres. Its specialised bed strength has been revised from 108 to 117. It will have 65 adult beds and 52 infant beds. The block will house specialties of gynae-oncology and assisted fertility and will house specialised healthcare infrastructure. This includes modular operation theatres, intensive care units, high-dependency units, neonatal intensive care facilities, Labour, Delivery and Recovery suites, IVF laboratories and advanced foetal intervention facilities. Component-wise progress shows civil works at 75 percent. On the same lines, electrical works have been completed 78 percent while mechanical works are at 71 percent. Sixty-two percent medical equipment has been procured. The agreement for execution of the project was signed on August 1, 2025. The original completion deadline was December 31, 2026, and now the revised completion date has been fixed as February 28, 2027. The project is part of the reconstruction and augmentation of critical hospital infrastructure under the World Bank-funded JTFRP. The proposal was approved in 2017, but the project subsequently faced prolonged delays.

stories.headline: Govt to revive Kashmir’s only olive cultivation belt
stories.title: Govt to revive Kashmir’s only olive cultivation belt
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 24: The government has constituted a committee to revive Kashmir’s only established olive cultivation belt in the Salamabad area of Uri in north Kashmir’s Baramulla district, which is facing a gradual decline due to the prolonged absence of a reliable irrigation facility. The 29-kanal olive plantation, located near the Line of Control (LoC), has been struggling for years as the lack of adequate water supply has affected the growth and productivity of trees, raising concerns over the future of the region’s unique olive-growing legacy. Joint Director Horticulture Kashmir Javaid Bhat told Rising Kashmir that the department has constituted a committee comprising four to five officials to explore measures for reviving the plantation. “I have constituted a committee comprising four to five officials, who are working on ways to revive the olive belt,” he said. Bhat said the department was also planning to introduce new rows of olive trees, experiment with other crops and explore high-density plantations to improve productivity. He said efforts were being made to identify a sustainable source of irrigation, including the possibility of lifting water from the Jhelum River to irrigate the orchard. Another horticulture department official said the department had approached the Irrigation Department in Uri to explore the possibility of lifting water from the river, but the proposal had not received a positive response. “We are now planning to approach NHPC authorities, which have a reservoir near the olive plantation, and request their intervention to help restore the irrigation facility,” the official said. He said the prolonged absence of irrigation had considerably affected the health and productivity of olive trees. “The growth and productivity of olive trees have reduced considerably. Without a dependable source of irrigation, sustaining the plantation has become increasingly difficult,” the official said. The plantation was established in 1987 under an Indo-Italian collaboration and initially had access to a natural stream. Water from the stream was collected in a tank and subsequently used to irrigate the orchard. However, the 2005 earthquake damaged the water supply system, leaving the plantation without a reliable irrigation source. Since then, rainfall has remained the primary source of moisture for the trees, contributing to a gradual decline in their growth and yield. The department has also explored alternative ways to restore irrigation. In 2024, the Irrigation Department inspected the site to assess the feasibility of developing a groundwater source. “They had proposed digging a borewell, but the plan could not be implemented because of the area’s higher elevation, which makes groundwater extraction technically difficult,” the official said. The irrigation crisis has affected not only olive production but also the broader objective of promoting olive oil extraction in the region. Olive cultivation in Kashmir remains largely confined to the Uri region, where relatively warmer climatic conditions and suitable soil have provided a favourable environment for the Mediterranean crop. The Salamabad plantation was established after soil studies conducted by a British team identified the area as suitable for olive cultivation. The project was subsequently taken up in 1987 under an Indo-Italian collaboration as an important initiative to diversify horticulture in the region. Local residents and growers have expressed concern over the gradual deterioration of the plantation, saying immediate government intervention is necessary to prevent Kashmir's only established olive-growing belt from further decline.

stories.headline: CS Yadav pushes for faster project execution without compromising quality
stories.title: CS Yadav pushes for faster project execution without compromising quality
stories.summary: Rajouri, Nov 24: Chief Secretary Sajjan Singh Yadav on Sunday emphasised expedited execution of development projects with no compromise on quality at any stage. He also stressed the importance of academic programmes and degrees aligning with employability and skill development. He asserted this while interacting with the project executing agencies and students during his extensive tour of Rajouri district. The visit was aimed at reviewing the progress of key developmental projects, assessing sports and educational infrastructure, inspecting healthcare and power facilities and taking stock of restoration works at important historical sites. During his morning visit to the Sports Stadium, Rajouri, the Chief Secretary interacted with young sportspersons participating in various disciplines, including volleyball and badminton and sought their feedback regarding the availability of sports facilities and coaching arrangements. Appreciating the sporting talent of the district, he emphasised the need to provide aspiring players with better infrastructure, professional coaching and adequate opportunities to excel at higher levels. He stressed the need for engaging more coaches in the district under the Khelo India initiative to nurture local talent and enable promising sportspersons to compete at national and international levels. The Chief Secretary also inspected the ongoing construction works at the Sports Stadium, Kheora and directed the concerned authorities to ensure their expeditious execution while maintaining the prescribed quality standards for optimal utilisation of the facilities. Reviews Developmental Works at BGSBU At Baba Ghulam Shah Badshah University (BGSBU), Rajouri, the Chief Secretary inspected the ongoing construction of the university auditorium, Girls Hostel for Nursing Students and the new main gate. He was apprised that the girls' hostel, being constructed at an allotted cost of Rs 354.23 lakh, achieved completion of masonry work on its ground and first floors, with plastering presently underway. Similarly, the superstructure of the new university main gate, being executed at an allotted cost of Rs 59.11 lakh, was completed, while the remaining works were in progress. Directing the executing agencies to accelerate the pace of construction, he underscored that quality should not be compromised at any stage. He also emphasised the installation of rooftop solar power plants in new university buildings to promote renewable energy, enhance energy efficiency and reduce dependence on conventional power sources. Later, at the university's IT Hall, the Chief Secretary interacted with students, faculty members and university functionaries. The interaction was attended by Vice Chancellor, BGSBU, Prof Jawaid Iqbal; Deputy Commissioner, Rajouri, Dr Devansh Yadav; DIG Sandeep Wazir; ADDC Malik Zada Sheraz Ul Haq; Registrar, ADC Ravi Sihag; SSP Naresh Singh; Dean Academics and other senior officers. At the outset, the Registrar presented an overview of the university, highlighting student enrolment, academic programmes, courses offered and its overall functioning. Addressing the gathering, Yadav appreciated the university's contribution to higher education and called upon its administration, faculty and students to work collectively towards taking the institution to greater heights of academic excellence. He stressed the need for formulating a clear ten-year vision for the university, supported by well-defined goals, measurable objectives and a comprehensive action plan involving all stakeholders. He further emphasised that academic programmes and degrees must remain aligned with employability, skill development and emerging opportunities in the job market. Encouraging students to pursue continuous learning, he called upon them to acquire knowledge and skills beyond the prescribed academic curriculum to emerge as capable, confident and responsible individuals. Reviews Healthcare and Power Infrastructure The Chief Secretary also inspected the 180-bedded Teaching District Hospital building at Rajouri, completed under the original project component and reviewed the progress of additional civil, electrical and mechanical works being undertaken at an additional approved cost of Rs 5 Cr. He was informed that the civil works were completed, electrical works were nearing completion, installation of lifts was completed, while firefighting works were presently in progress. He directed the concerned authorities to expedite the remaining works and ensure early operational readiness of the hospital facility so that the people of the district could benefit from enhanced healthcare infrastructure. He also visited the 6.3 MVA Dedicated Receiving Station being constructed at Government Medical College (GMC), Rajouri with the work having been awarded at Rs 2.89 Cr. The project, being executed by STD Division-IV, Kalakote, is targeted for completion by March 2027. During the inspection, he was informed that approximately 90 per cent of the ground-floor building work had been completed, while the SBA quarter had achieved 35 per cent progress. The foundations for the power transformer and associated equipment have also been laid, and material inspection has been completed. The Chief Secretary observed that commissioning of the dedicated receiving station would substantially strengthen the power infrastructure of GMC Rajouri and ensure improved reliability and quality of electricity supply, which was critical for uninterrupted healthcare services. He stressed the importance of adhering to the stipulated timeline for its completion. Inspects Flood-Damaged Infrastructure, Reviews Connectivity Projects Taking stock of the damage caused to public infrastructure by recent flash floods, the Chief Secretary visited Bella Bus Stand, which had been washed away and assessed the restoration requirements. He emphasised the need for appropriate rehabilitation measures and early restoration of the facility in the larger public interest. At Androlla bridge, he directed the executing agency to complete the pending works at the earliest to ensure timely restoration of connectivity and facilitate the movement of the local population. Calls for Conservation of Historical Chingus Sarai During his visit to the historic Chingus Sarai, an important heritage site historically used by the Mughals as a transit camp during their annual journeys to Kashmir, the Chief Secretary reviewed the proposed restoration and preservation plan estimated at Rs 175.75 lakh. He was informed that limestone would be used in the restoration process. Emphasising the historical and architectural significance of the site, he directed the concerned authorities to undertake the restoration strictly in accordance with its original architectural character, ensuring that the existing structure and heritage value remain undisturbed. Pays Tributes to Dr Raj Kumar Thapa The Chief Secretary also visited Dr Raj Kumar Thapa Memorial, Museum and Library at the official residential quarter where he had attained martyrdom during Operation Sindoor while performing his official duties. He paid floral tributes to the martyr and recalled his supreme sacrifice in the line of duty, observing that his courage, dedication and commitment to public service would continue to inspire generations. While inspecting the library established within the memorial complex, he directed the concerned authorities to ensure the availability of a diverse collection of age-appropriate books for children visiting the facility, so that it could serve as a meaningful centre for reading, learning and knowledge. Throughout the visit, the Chief Secretary underscored the importance of timely completion of developmental projects, strict adherence to quality standards, effective utilisation of public assets and close monitoring by the concerned departments and executing agencies. “The Chief Secretary’s extensive field visits underscore his commitment to strengthening on-ground monitoring and ensuring balanced development across J&K, with focused attention on quality infrastructure, improved public services, youth empowerment, better connectivity and preservation of rich cultural and historical heritage across different regions of the UT,” it was stated.

stories.headline: Warwan glacial lake threatens downstream villages
stories.title: Warwan glacial lake threatens downstream villages
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 22: An expanding glacial lake in Kishtwar's remote Warwan Valley poses a potential flood threat to downstream villages in Warwan and Marwah, while raising concerns over hydropower infrastructure farther downstream in Kishtwar district, according to a new scientific study. A worst-case simulation shows that an avalanche striking Lake-B in the Fariabaad Nalla catchment could release 97.5 percent of its stored water, generating a peak discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second immediately below the lake. The resulting flood could travel about 65 km and reach a point just upstream of Qaderna village in Marwah Valley within six hours. The study identifies nine bridges, 40 buildings and several road networks within the potential inundation zone, particularly along the Marusudar River, a major tributary of the Chenab, near Yurod and Qaderna. It also examines the potential exposure of Kishtwar's Bursar (800 MW) and Pakal Dul (1000 MW) hydropower projects, located around 90 km downstream of the glacier complex. However, both projects lie beyond the study's 85-km flood-routing domain, and the researchers did not simulate flood arrival at either site or quantify possible damage. Published on November 4, 2026, in the journal Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, the study reconstructs an avalanche-triggered glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in September 2020 and assesses the potential consequences of a future outburst from another lake in the Warwan sub-basin. Worst-case scenario could release 97.5% of lake water The researchers modelled three scenarios involving avalanches of different magnitudes striking Lake-B. In the worst-case scenario, a 25-million-cubic-metre rock-ice avalanche entering the lake could generate a peak water discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second. The avalanche debris could add another 1316 cubic metres per second to the flow immediately below the lake. The simulation estimates that 97.5 percent of the lake's stored water could be released. A moderate avalanche could drain 91 percent, while a lower-magnitude event could release about 85.7 percent. Further downstream, peak discharge could reach 621 cubic metres per second at a section 49 km from the lake before declining to 535 cubic metres per second near Qaderna, approximately 65 km downstream, by the sixth hour. Maximum flow depths at these two locations were estimated at 2.8 metres and 2 metres. At locations with infrastructure, the model indicated possible flow depths of two to four metres and velocities of four to six metres per second. The researchers cautioned that the simulations represent potential scenarios, not a prediction that an outburst will occur. 2020 avalanche triggered GLOF from Lake-A The study reconstructed an earlier event in September 2020, when a rock-ice avalanche struck Lake-A, displacing its stored water and sediment and triggering a GLOF followed by a downstream debris flow. The avalanche originated from the accumulation zone of glacier GL-A at an altitude of about 4890 metres. It travelled 2355 metres and covered a mapped area of around 0.78 sq km. Satellite imagery taken before and after the event showed that the lake's moraine was breached, its outlet channel widened and debris was deposited downstream. According to the researchers, sediment carried by meltwater streams from adjoining glaciers GL-D and GL-E had gradually accumulated in Lake-A, dividing it into two basins. The avalanche impact displaced the stored water and sediment, sending the material downstream. The outburst did not trigger a second GLOF from Lake-B, located immediately downstream. A smaller proglacial lake later re-formed at the terminus of GL-A. The study also documented two other major avalanche events in the glacier complex. An avalanche in September 2005 originated from the headwall of glacier GL-B and travelled about 2620 metres but stopped before reaching its lake. In March 2020, a rock-ice avalanche from glacier GL-F travelled around 2,470 metres, affecting an area of about 1.24 sq km, but did not reach a glacial lake. Lake-B expands 308% in 25 years Satellite imagery showed that Lake-B expanded from about 0.07 sq km in 1999 to 0.306 sq km in 2024, an increase of approximately 308 percent. The researchers attributed the expansion to glacier retreat, meltwater inflow and repeated ice-calving events. A reconstruction of the glacier bed placed the lake's potential maximum volume at 7.7 million cubic metres, while a separate volume-area scaling method produced a comparable estimate of 7.4 million cubic metres. The wider Fariabaad catchment covers 1404 sq km, with an average elevation of 4308 metres. It contains 272 glaciers spread over 315 sq km. The number of glacial lakes in the catchment increased from seven in 1990 to 12. Settlements, infrastructure along flood path The researchers identified Qaderna, Yurod, Anyar, Rinaie and Metwan among the settlements located around 50-55 km downstream of the glacier complex. These settlements lie in the downstream Marwah valley region, with settlements and agricultural activity also extending farther along the Marusudar River in Kishtwar district. The study noted that new settlements and agricultural activity have emerged along riverbanks over the past two decades, increasing the number of people and assets exposed to potential flooding. The Bursar and Pakal Dul hydropower projects, situated around 90 kilometres downstream, were also considered in the broader assessment of infrastructure exposure. However, their location beyond the 85-km flood-routing domain means the study does not establish whether floodwaters would reach either facility. The researchers also warned that a future GLOF could trigger cascading hazards, including debris flows and temporary river blockages. Large volumes of loose sediment deposited along the valley could be remobilised by floodwaters, amplifying the impact farther downstream. They recommended stronger monitoring, comprehensive hazard inventories and preparedness measures across the remote catchment. "An early warning system closer to the source could provide valuable lead time during a potential outburst," the researchers said. They also called for community-level preparedness and urged authorities to factor GLOF risks into infrastructure development and land-use planning. opening: Srinagar, Nov 22: An expanding glacial lake in Kishtwar's remote Warwan Valley poses a potential flood threat to downstream villages in Warwan and Marwah, while raising concerns over hydropower infrastructure farther downstream in Kishtwar district, according to a new scientific study.

A worst-case simulation shows that an avalanche striking Lake-B in the Fariabaad Nalla catchment could release 97.5 percent of its stored water, generating a peak discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second immediately below the lake.
body: The resulting flood could travel about 65 km and reach a point just upstream of Qaderna village in Marwah Valley within six hours.

The study identifies nine bridges, 40 buildings and several road networks within the potential inundation zone, particularly along the Marusudar River, a major tributary of the Chenab, near Yurod and Qaderna.
It also examines the potential exposure of Kishtwar's Bursar (800 MW) and Pakal Dul (1000 MW) hydropower projects, located around 90 km downstream of the glacier complex.
However, both projects lie beyond the study's 85-km flood-routing domain, and the researchers did not simulate flood arrival at either site or quantify possible damage.

Published on November 4, 2026, in the journal Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, the study reconstructs an avalanche-triggered glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in September 2020 and assesses the potential consequences of a future outburst from another lake in the Warwan sub-basin.
Worst-case scenario could release 97.5% of lake water.

The researchers modelled three scenarios involving avalanches of different magnitudes striking Lake-B. In the worst-case scenario, a 25-million-cubic-metre rock-ice avalanche entering the lake could generate a peak water discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second.
The avalanche debris could add another 1316 cubic metres per second to the flow immediately below the lake.
The simulation estimates that 97.5 percent of the lake's stored water could be released.

Further downstream, peak discharge could reach 621 cubic metres per second at a section 49 km from the lake before declining to 535 cubic metres per second near Qaderna, approximately 65 km downstream, by the sixth hour.
Maximum flow depths at these two locations were estimated at 2.8 metres and 2 metres.
At locations with infrastructure, the model indicated possible flow depths of two to four metres and velocities of four to six metres per second.
The researchers cautioned that the simulations represent potential scenarios, not a prediction that an outburst will occur.

2020 avalanche triggered GLOF from Lake-A. The study reconstructed an earlier event in September 2020, when a rock-ice avalanche struck Lake-A, displacing its stored water and sediment and triggering a GLOF followed by a downstream debris flow.
The avalanche originated from the accumulation zone of glacier GL-A at an altitude of about 4890 metres.
It travelled 2355 metres and covered a mapped area of around 0.78 sq km.
Satellite imagery taken before and after the event showed that the lake's moraine was breached, its outlet channel widened and debris was deposited downstream.
According to the researchers, sediment carried by meltwater streams from adjoining glaciers GL-D and GL-E had gradually accumulated in Lake-A, dividing it into two basins.
The avalanche impact displaced the stored water and sediment, sending the material downstream.
The outburst did not trigger a second GLOF from Lake-B, located immediately downstream.
A smaller proglacial lake later re-formed at the terminus of GL-A. The study also documented two other major avalanche events in the glacier complex.
An avalanche in September 2005 originated from the headwall of glacier GL-B and travelled about 2620 metres but stopped before reaching its lake.
The researchers attributed the expansion to glacier retreat, meltwater inflow and repeated ice-calving events.

A reconstruction of the glacier bed placed the lake's potential maximum volume at 7.7 million cubic metres, while a separate volume-area scaling method produced a comparable estimate of 7.4 million cubic metres.
The wider Fariabaad catchment covers 1404 sq km, with an average elevation of 4308 metres.
It contains 272 glaciers spread over 315 sq km.
The number of glacial lakes in the catchment increased from seven in 1990 to 12.
Settlements, infrastructure along flood path.
These settlements lie in the downstream Marwah valley region, with settlements and agricultural activity also extending farther along the Marusudar River in Kishtwar district.
The study noted that new settlements and agricultural activity have emerged along riverbanks over the past two decades, increasing the number of people and assets exposed to potential flooding.
The Bursar and Pakal Dul hydropower projects, situated around 90 kilometres downstream, were also considered in the broader assessment of infrastructure exposure.
However, their location beyond the 85-km flood-routing domain means the study does not establish whether floodwaters would reach either facility.
The researchers also warned that a future GLOF could trigger cascading hazards, including debris flows and temporary river blockages.
Large volumes of loose sediment deposited along the valley could be remobilised by floodwaters, amplifying the impact farther downstream.
They recommended stronger monitoring, comprehensive hazard inventories and preparedness measures across the remote catchment.
"An early warning system closer to the source could provide valuable lead time during a potential outburst," the researchers said.
They also called for community-level preparedness and urged authorities to factor GLOF risks into infrastructure development and land-use planning.

The study, titled Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya, was authored by Ashim Sattar and Abhinav Alangadan of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar; Shashi Kant Rai and Sunil Dhar of the Central University of Jammu; Adam Emmer of Charles University, Prague, and the University of Graz, Austria; Umesh Haritashya of the University of Dayton, US; and M. Farooq Azam of IIT Indore.

stories.headline: Book on drug abuse, prevention released in Banihal
stories.title: Book on drug abuse, prevention released in Banihal
stories.summary: Banihal, Nov 24: A book titled “Drug abuse: Causes and prevention”, authored by Banihal-based writer Manzoor Ahmad Wani Banihali, was released at a special function organised by the Social Welfare Association Banihal (SWAB) at Government Boys Higher Secondary School here on Tuesday. MLA Banihal-Gool Haji Sajjad Shaheen presided over the function, while Deputy Commissioner Ramban Mohammad Alyas Khan attended as the chief guest. Prominent writer and poet Manshoor Banihali was the guest of honour. The event witnessed the participation of a large number of intellectuals, writers, social activists and people from different walks of life. Several local Jammu and Kashmir Administrative Service (JKAS) officers from Banihal, currently posted in different parts of Jammu and Kashmir, including Vikar Ahmed Giri, Bashir-ul-Hassan, Bilal Shamas Kamgar and Tanveer-ul-Majeed, also attended the function. The book explores the growing drug menace from social, psychological, moral and educational perspectives, highlighting its devastating impact on youth, families and society. A nine-minute documentary, compiled and edited by Athar Mujtaba Wani, nephew of the author, was also screened during the programme. The film, highlighting the causes, consequences and preventive measures against drug abuse, was formally presented by the author's father, Abdul Majeed Wani. Former Chief Justice of India Justice Tirath Singh Thakur, in his remarks on the book, described drug abuse as a serious challenge requiring more than legal action, emphasising the importance of treatment, psychological support, education and public awareness. Noted writer and poet Manshoor Banihali also appreciated the publication, describing it as an important social and moral initiative. Congratulating the author, MLA Sajjad Shaheen described the book as an informative and research-oriented effort on an issue of immense social importance. He assured support for making it available in school and educational institution libraries and stressed the need for its English translation to widen its reach. He also said he would take up the matter with the Education Minister and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to explore its introduction in educational institutions. DC Ramban Mohammad Alyas Khan appreciated the author and the organisers, describing drug abuse as a serious global social challenge that required coordinated efforts by parents, educational institutions, civil society and government agencies. A paper highlighting various aspects of the book and the drug abuse problem was also presented during the function. Speaking on the occasion, author Manzoor Ahmad Wani Banihali said the book was dedicated to parents concerned about their children's future and their protection from substance abuse. He stressed that people suffering from addiction should not be subjected to social hatred, discrimination or isolation, but should instead be provided treatment, counselling and rehabilitation. However, strict legal action must be taken against those involved in the illegal drug trade. The author expressed gratitude to all participants, members of the Social Welfare Association Banihal, the Principal of Government Boys Higher Secondary School Banihal and the district and sub-divisional administrations for their support and cooperation in making the event successful. The programme concluded with a call for collective community participation in combating drug abuse and safeguarding the future of the younger generation.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Issues Notice On Plea Challenging Exclusion Of Released Women Officers From Indian Coast Guard Permanent Absorption
stories.title: Supreme Court Issues Notice On Plea Challenging Exclusion Of Released Women Officers From Indian Coast Guard Permanent Absorption
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court recently issued notice on the plea filed by a woman Indian Coast Guard officer, released from service, challenging the ICG policy which allowed SSA women officers of the General Duty branch to opt for Permanent Appointment.

The policy is contested on the ground that it unfairly limits the option to officers "in service as on date", excluding officers like the petitioner who were released on completion of the maximum SSA engagement (14 years) before the policy was issued.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order, issuing notice to the Union and Director General of ICG.

Advocates Siddhant Sharma, Prafull Bhardwaj and Snehil Himanshi appeared for the petitioner, ex-commandant (JG) Priyanka, who served in the Coast Guard for 14 years before being released in December 2023.
Briefly put, the petition challenges policy letters dated 18.08.2026, which for the first time allowed women SSA officers of the General Duty branch to opt for permanent appointment.
As per claims, the petitioner joined the Coast Guard on 30.12.2009 as part of the pioneer SSA (GD) course.
In March 2023, she formally made a request for permanent absorption.
Her request was recommended at every level in the chain of command, with superiors suggesting a policy change if needed.
However no decision was conveyed before her release in 2023.

The petition refers to an eligible officer (Priyanka Tyagi) under the new policy who hails from the same batch as the petitioner (December 2009), underlining that she was also released from service in 2023 but continues in service as on date because of Supreme Court's interim order [Ref: Priyanka Tyagi.
It is also claimed that 11 out of 36 eligible officers listed in the petition had crossed 14 years of service before the impugned policy was issued.

stories.headline: Amit Shah: Kartarpur corridor to open after review
stories.title: Amit Shah: Kartarpur corridor to open after review
stories.summary: Union home minister Amit Shah expressed that the Kartarpur Sahib Corridor will only reopen after addressing prevailing security issues. This corridor, which offers hassle-free access for pilgrims, was shut down following security alerts linked to Operation Sindoor. Shah highlighted the need to keep national security discussions free from political influences, while also pointing out that the corridor's placement in Pakistan stemmed from Congress party oversights during partition.

stories.headline: NSA Ajit Doval, Maldives defence minister discuss security ties at Colombo meet
stories.title: NSA Ajit Doval, Maldives defence minister discuss security ties at Colombo meet
stories.summary: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Maldives defense minister Hassan Rasheed discussed security cooperation at the Colombo Security Conclave. This meeting marked the first high-level interaction between the two countries since President Mohamed Muizzu's recent visit to Pakistan. During that visit, Maldives signed 20 agreements with Pakistan related to defense and maritime issues. Additionally, Muizzu called for resuming the Saarc summit process to enhance regional cooperation.
